title: The knight in a busy position, on the edge and in the corner
outcomes: Names the piece on a given square before using its rule, with no hint in the prompt
Taps every square a knight can jump to in a crowded position, leaving out squares held by its own pieces
Counts fewer than eight jumps for a knight on the edge or in the corner
Says that pieces beside the knight do not block it
Explains why a knight check cannot be blocked
Checks whether an enemy pawn attacks a landing square before jumping there

steps.text: Here is a way to be sure. List the knight's eight possible jumps, then cross out the ones that do not work: a jump that would leave the board, and a jump onto one of its own pieces. A jump onto an enemy piece stays in, because that is a capture. The next board does exactly this for the knight you just met.

steps.caption: Eight candidates around d4. Only c2 is crossed out: a white pawn stands there. Four landing squares hold black pieces, and each is a capture, so they stay in.

line.say: Landing on a square with a black piece is a capture. Here the knight takes the bishop on e6.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 has exactly these seven landing squares.

steps.caption: At the start the knight on b1 has three candidates: a3, c3 and d2. The pawn on d2 is its own, so d2 is crossed out. The pawns directly in front of the knight change nothing.

line.say: The knight jumps over its own pawns and lands on c3, nearer the middle.

claims.statement: The knight on b1 can go to exactly a3 and c3.

steps.caption: The bishop on c1 has no move yet: its own pawns on b2 and d2 block both diagonals. The knight beside it is free. Pieces between never block a knight; the landing square decides. Later you will meet pins, where a knight cannot move at all.

claims.statement: The bishop on c1 has no legal move at the start.
The knight on b1 has two legal moves.

steps.caption: Now the knight stands on c3, and Black has moved a knight too. Eight candidates: a2 and e2 hold white pawns and d1 holds the queen, so three are crossed out. Five jumps remain, one of them back to b1.

line.say: Jumping to e4 puts the knight in the centre of the board.

claims.statement: The knight on c3 has exactly five legal jumps.

steps.caption: The knight on d4 cannot jump to f5, because its own bishop stands there. But it defends that bishop. If the rook takes the bishop, the knight takes the rook back.

line.say: The rook takes the bishop.
The knight takes the rook. A crossed-out square is still a square the knight defends.

claims.statement: One white piece, the knight, defends the bishop on f5.
One black piece, the rook, attacks the bishop on f5.
No white piece is loose.

steps.caption: Start in the middle. On d4 the knight has all eight jumps, because every landing square is on the board.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 has eight legal jumps.

steps.caption: One step in from the edge, on b3, two of the eight jumps would land off the board. Six remain.

line.say: One jump brings it back to the middle, where it has eight again.

claims.statement: The knight on b3 has exactly six jumps.

steps.caption: On the edge, on a4, half of the jumps would leave the board. Four remain.

line.say: Even from the edge, one jump toward the middle gives the knight room again.

claims.statement: The knight on a4 has exactly four jumps.

steps.caption: In the corner, on a1, only two jumps stay on the board. Watch how many jumps it takes to get out.

line.say: The first jump leaves the corner.
Black's king steps aside; nothing here threatens the knight.
The second jump reaches the centre, where it has eight jumps again.

claims.statement: The knight on a1 has exactly two jumps.

steps.text: Four examples from the boards you just saw: the middle gave eight jumps, one step in six, the edge four, the corner two. These are examples, not a law: nearer an edge or corner means fewer jumps, and squares next to a corner have three. Counted over all 64 squares [V]: 2 jumps on 4 squares, 3 on 8, 4 on 20, 6 on 16, 8 on 16.

[I] A centre knight is stronger because more jumps mean more threats and more retreats. [H] I would treat the edge as a reason to count your exits, not as a ban. *Quick count:* start at the square two up and one right, then go clockwise round the knight: eight stops, none missed. Cross out each stop that is off the board or holds your own piece.

steps.caption: The knight starts on a light square. After one jump it stands on a dark square, after the next on a light one again. Every jump changes the colour of the square, so a knight on a light square attacks only dark squares.

line.say: From light to dark.
Black's king waits.
From dark to light again.

claims.statement: The knight on b1 has exactly three jumps.
The knight can jump to c3.

steps.caption: This knight on h4 is on the edge. Four jumps are possible, but its own pawns on f3 and g2 take two of them away. Two are left.

line.say: From g6 the knight has plenty of exits again, towards the middle. An edge knight is cramped, not lost.

claims.statement: The knight on h4 can go to exactly f5 and g6.

steps.title: Centre, edge, neighbours
steps.prompt: Predict first. Count the knight's jumps in each of the three positions. Which counts differ, and why?

steps.caption: Black's knight is on a8 with two jumps, b6 and c7. The white pawn on a5 attacks b6 and the rook on c1 attacks c7. The bishop on f3 attacks the knight itself.

line.say: The knight tries b6.
The pawn takes it. Both exits lead into an attack, so the knight is trapped.

claims.statement: The knight on a8 has exactly two jumps.
One white piece attacks b6.
One white piece attacks c7.
One white piece attacks the knight.

steps.caption: Take away the white pawn on e5 and the same knight has an exit. f6 is attacked by nothing, so the knight can jump there and be safe.

line.say: f6 is free of attackers, so the knight escapes toward the middle.

claims.statement: The knight on h5 has three jumps.
No white piece attacks f6.
The pawn on e3 attacks f4.
The pawn on h2 attacks g3.

steps.text: A jump has nothing in between, and that gives the knight two special powers. A check from a knight cannot be blocked. And a knight can attack a piece that cannot attack it back. Watch the first power next to an ordinary check, with the same king and bishop.

steps.caption: White's rook on e1 gives check along the e-file. Black has an answer besides moving the king: the bishop can stand in between.

line.say: The bishop steps between the rook and the king and blocks the check.

claims.statement: Black is in check.
The bishop can legally step to e6.

steps.caption: Now a knight on d6 gives check. A jump has no squares in between, so nothing can be put in the way. Black's bishop has moves, but none of them is legal now. Only the king may move. The pawn on c5 guards the knight.

line.say: The king has to move. A knight check can only be answered by moving the king or taking the knight.

claims.statement: Black is in check.
The bishop cannot legally go to e6.
The bishop cannot legally go to c6.
The only legal moves are king moves.

steps.caption: The queen on d6 is worth far more than a knight. White's rook guards the back rank, so Black has no mate threat. The knight can jump to a square an L away from the queen, and no queen attacks along an L.

line.say: The knight attacks the queen, and the queen cannot take it.
The queen has to run away.

claims.statement: After the jump the knight attacks the queen.
After the jump no black piece attacks the knight.
If White passed, Black's queen move to d1 would give check but not mate, because the rook takes it.

steps.caption: A double attack means one piece attacks two targets at once. Here a knight jump will give check and attack the queen on c8 in the same move.

line.say: Check, and the queen is attacked too.
The king steps aside.
The knight takes the queen.

claims.statement: The knight can jump to e7.
After the jump the knight attacks the king.
After the jump the knight attacks the queen.
The jump wins the queen.

steps.caption: Both sides bring a knight out early. On g1 the knight has three exits. One jump later it attacks the pawn on e5, and Black answers with a knight of its own that defends the pawn.

line.say: The knight comes out and attacks the pawn on e5.
Black's knight comes out too and defends that pawn.

claims.statement: The knight on g1 has exactly three jumps.
After the jump the knight attacks the pawn on e5.
After the reply a black knight defends the pawn.

steps.caption: On g1 the knight attacks 3 squares; on f3 it attacks 8, including the centre squares d4 and e5 (it also defends its own pieces on d2, e1 and h2). From g1 it did none of this.

claims.statement: The knight on f3 attacks exactly these eight squares.

steps.text: Our own data [V]: of 329,008 first moves in our master games (both players rated 2500 or higher), 38,956 were Nf3. After 1.e4 e5, White played Nf3 in 53,390 of 56,809 games.

Views [S]: Capablanca (*Chess Fundamentals*) and Emanuel Lasker (*Common Sense in Chess*) both treated knights before bishops as a default, not a law.

[H] A guess: a knight has few useful squares, so its best square is decided sooner than a bishop's, which depends on the pawns.

steps.caption: The knight on c3 has six jumps. Two of them, b5 and d5, are legal but dangerous: the pawn on c6 attacks both, and the pawn on e6 attacks d5 as well.

line.say: The knight lands on d5, where two pawns attack it.
A pawn takes the knight. A knight is worth more than a pawn, so Black is happy.

claims.statement: The knight on c3 has exactly six legal jumps.
Two black pawns attack d5.
One black pawn attacks b5.
Jumping to d5 loses material compared with the best move.

steps.text: A jump can be legal and still be a mistake. Before you jump, ask what attacks the landing square. A pawn is the usual surprise, because a pawn is worth much less than a knight. *Rule of thumb:* first check the landing square, then think about the target.

steps.caption: The count assumes the knight is free to move. Here Black's knight stands between its king and the rook, so it is pinned: any jump would expose the king, and the knight has no legal move at all.

claims.statement: The pinned knight on e6 has no legal move.
The rook attacks the knight.

steps.text: Six checks with no hints are next. Count the exits first, then ask of each landing square what attacks it. A knight that has exits but no safe ones is in as much trouble as one with none.

steps.prompt: Explain to a friend how to count a knight's jumps: what you cross out, what you keep, and one warning. Write it in your own words before you read on.

steps.text: **Check your explanation.** Did you say that the knight jumps in an L; that you cross out squares off the board and squares with your own pieces; that you keep captures; that pieces between never block; that edge and corner knights have fewer jumps; and that you check what attacks the landing square? Add whatever you missed.
